info.bio: Benny Goodman (Chicago, 30 de mayo de 1909 – Nueva York, 13 de junio de 1986) -nacido como Benjamin David Goodman- fue un clarinetista y director de jazz estadounidense. Conocido como "el rey del swing", es, junto con Glenn Miller y Count Basie, el máximo representante de este estilo jazzístico. Director de una de las big band más populares de su época, desarrolló sobre todo la variante más suave del género, la de las sweet bands, y fue el iniciador de la llamada era del swing.

scenes.name: El Renacimiento de Harlem y el swing
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Inspirado por el nacionalismo negro de Marcus Garvey («Up you mighty race!»), el Renacimiento de Harlem buscó la sofisticación frente a los estereotipos racistas, con una casta interna (ciudad contra campo, claros contra oscuros) que miraba por encima del hombro el blues rural, es decir, lo funky. Cab Calloway y luego Louis Jordan encarnaron al líder de banda que se mueve al compás y rapea percusivamente. El swing de los treinta, orquestado y estructurado, se alejó de sus raíces hasta que los blancos lo tocaron igual: Benny Goodman y Paul Whiteman se llevaron el dinero, y Ted Vincent lo llama «el disco de los años treinta».
scenes.family: Raíces: blues, jazz, gospel y R&B

scenes.name: Jazz de Chicago: Condon y la Austin High Gang
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La geografía del primer jazz no es un triángulo fluvial: el Mississippi pasa lejos de Chicago y Armstrong llegó en tren; el fonógrafo, y luego la radio, son tan decisivos como los músicos. Unos estudiantes blancos del barrio de Austin descubren a los New Orleans Rhythm Kings en una gramola y forman los Blue Friars; con Eddie Condon, ideólogo, cronista y epigramista («los músicos de bop disminuyen las quintas; nosotros nos las bebemos»), crean el mito del jazzman antihéroe. Su música es más tensa: las líneas compiten en lugar de entrelazarse, el saxo tenor sustituye al trombón, hay introducciones escritas, flare ups y explosiones, y ecos de klezmer, violín callejero o música clásica moderna. Frank Teschemacher, Bud Freeman, Gene Krupa, Pee Wee Russell (Dixieland y Dadá), Adrian Rollini con su saxo bajo, el «estilo neoyorquino» de Red Nichols y Miff Mole, y Jack Teagarden, trombonista y cantante de blues, íntimo como Crosby.

scenes.name: Benny Goodman, el rey del swing
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La Depresión hunde la venta de discos y el fin de la ley seca desmitifica el jazz, pero la radio en cadena crea el estrellato: managers como Hammond, Glaser o Mills median entre arte y masas. Goodman, hijo de inmigrantes judíos de Maxwell Street y clarinetista de técnica clásica, prepara su triunfo en el programa Let's Dance de la NBC (con arreglos de Fletcher Henderson, «King Porter Stomp», «Sometimes I'm Happy») y estalla en el Palomar Ballroom el 21 de agosto de 1935: nace la era del swing y el fenómeno de fans que anuncia a Sinatra, Elvis o los Beatles. Con Hammond rompe la barrera racial en sus combos (Teddy Wilson, Lionel Hampton, Charlie Christian), lleva el jazz al Carnegie Hall en 1938 y encarga obras a Bartók, Copland y Hindemith. Gene Krupa populariza al batería como estrella; Bunny Berigan, Harry James, Ziggy Elman, Jess Stacy y luego Mel Powell y Eddie Sauter dan a la banda una modernidad propia, la que el bebop no siguió. Las bandas blancas tuvieron ventajas que Henderson nunca tuvo.

scenes.name: Charlie Christian y la guitarra eléctrica
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Un chico de Oklahoma City que tocaba en el Ritz Cafe por siete dólares y medio, recomendado por Mary Lou Williams a John Hammond: Goodman lo desdeña («un palurdo increíble») hasta que improvisan una hora sobre «Rose Room». En menos de dos años de grabaciones con el sexteto de Goodman define la guitarra eléctrica en el jazz con líneas de una sola nota, saltos interválicos, tresillos y tensiones cromáticas, frases que los guitarristas copiarán como un canon. Sus noches en el Minton's lo convierten en pionero del bebop; la tuberculosis lo mata en 1942.

scenes.name: Navarro, Dameron, Stitt y J. J. Johnson
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La primera generación que sigue a Bird y Dizzy. Sonny Stitt, el único contralto que se acerca a Parker en velocidad, rival temible en las jam sessions. Fats Navarro suaviza el lenguaje de Gillespie con un sonido más dulce y controlado y muere de tuberculosis a los veintiséis años. Tadd Dameron, compositor más que pianista bop, escribe piezas que entran en el repertorio («Hot House», «Good Bait», «Lady Bird», «If You Could See Me Now») y dirige en el Royal Roost una banda con Navarro y Kenny Clarke. J. J. Johnson traduce el bebop al trombón de varas, una hazaña técnica de la que dependen casi todos los trombonistas posteriores. Sarah Vaughan, salida de la banda de Hines de 1943, canta con espíritu instrumental, a lo Gillespie.

podcast.title: Carnegie Hall Integrated Performance (1938)
podcast.body: By 1938, Goodman achieved a significant milestone by bringing an integrated band, which included black musicians like Count Basie, Leste Jung, Teddy Wilson, and Lionel Hampton, alongside white musicians such as himself and Crouper, onto the prestigious stage of Carnegie Hall, the US's most renowned music venue at the time. "By 1938, Goodman actually reached the point where he was able to bring an integrated band, featuring Count Basie, Leste Jung, Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton. Plus other black musicians, along with white musicians such as Goodman and Crouper, onto the stage of Carnegie Hall, at the time the US's most prestigious music venue."

podcast.title: Early Adoption of Electric Guitars (1938)
podcast.body: Benny Goodman's band was among the early adopters of electric guitars around 1938, a time when these instruments were just beginning to establish their musical presence. "A lot of people started using them at the same time, like Benny Goodman's band, as we heard about in the first episode."

podcast.title: Sextet Formation (1939)
podcast.body: After Teddy Wilson and Dramagine Cooper departed in 1939, Goodman formed the Benny Goodman Sextet to compensate for the loss of these exceptional musicians. This rotating lineup revolved around three primary soloists: Goodman on clarinet, Hampton on vibraphone, and a new, highly influential addition, guitarist Charlie Christian. "But he also realised the need to make up for the loss of two such exceptional musicians by incorporating more, and so the Benny Goodman's sex sets were formed."

podcast.body: Benny Goodman purchased arrangements from Chick Webb's band, specifically from Edgar Sampson, a saxophone player and arranger, for many of his own band's biggest crowd-pleasers. "Goodman bought from Egg, a Sampson, the saxophone player who did most of Webb's arrangements."

podcast.title: Big Band Leader
podcast.body: Benny Goodman was recognized as a major band leader in the Big Band jazz scene. He directed large ensembles, and under the Big Band structure, all performers were subservient to the leader's artistic and musical authority. "These were orchestras of ten or more people led by a big name, Paul Whiteman, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections

podcast.title: Carnegie Hall Breakthrough
podcast.body: In early 1938, John Hammond promoted a concert by the Benny Goodman band at Carnegie Hall. This event was impressive as it marked the first time an integrated band had played at Carnegie Hall and the first time popular music had been treated as seriously as classical music. "It was the first time an integrated band had played Carnegie Hall, and the first time that popular music had been treated as seriously as classical music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 2: "Roll Em Pete" by Big Joe Turner

podcast.title: Classical Music Pioneer
podcast.body: Goodman was one of the first individuals to advocate for the mainstream acceptance of jazz music within the classical music world. This effort, aimed at integrating jazz into a conservative environment, co-existed with his equally radical push for the integration of musicians in his bands. "On the one hand, he was one of the first people to push for mainstream acceptance of jazz music in the classical music world, which would suggest trying to be as conservative as possible."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 1: "Flying Home", Benny Goodman, Charlie Christian, and Lionel Hampton

podcast.title: Flying Home as Prototypical Rock
podcast.body: The Benny Goodman Sextet's 1939 recording of "Flying Home" is described as almost a prototypical rock band, featuring piano, electric guitar, double bass, and drums—instruments that would become hallmarks of the rock genre 20 years later. It anticipated many aspects of rock, especially Charlie Christian's soloing, which was astonishingly advanced for its time. "Other than the vibraphone in clarinet, though, this small group was almost a prototypical rock band."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Initial Skepticism about Electric Guitar
podcast.body: Benny Goodman initially expressed strong reservations about the electric guitar, questioning its musical relevance before being persuaded by talent scout John Hammond to audition Charlie Christian. His reaction highlights the novelty and unfamiliarity of the instrument at the time. "Goodman wasn't really into it because, well, who the hell wants to hear an electric guitar, he apparently said."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

podcast.title: Instrumentalist Leader
podcast.body: Benny Goodman, the leader of the Benny Goodman Orchestra, was an instrumentalist (specifically, he played the clarinet) rather than a singer, a common characteristic of big bands where the focus was on the leader's instrumental prowess. "The Betty Goodman Orchestra... All of the leaders of the big bands were instrumentalists. They played clarinet, or trombone, or piano. They didn't sing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: King of Swing Association
podcast.body: Benny Goodman was the person most associated with the title "King of Swing" and held the name for the longest period. "Benny Goodman was the person most associated with the name, and he had the name longest."

podcast.title: King of Swing Title
podcast.body: Benny Goodman was widely known as the "King of Swing" and led the most popular of the three war swing bands. He was also an excellent clarinet player, blending his instrumental prowess with his leadership role. "Benny Goodman, the King of Swing, was the leader of the most popular of the three war swing bands, as well as being an excellent Clameneck player."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Musician Band Leader
podcast.body: Benny Goodman was an excellent musician and band leader, capable of holding his own on his instrument among most musicians. "Most of the big band leaders we remember now were themselves excellent musicians, Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Benny Goodman."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Pioneer of Integrated Bands
podcast.body: Goodman was one of the first band leaders to lead an integrated band during the segregation era, starting with a trio comprising himself (white and Jewish), drummer Dramagine Cooper (white), and pianist Teddy Wilson (black). This initiative, along with recruiting black arranger Fletcher Henderson, was largely spearheaded by his brother-in-law, John Hammond, a wealthy man dedicated to racial integration. "And importantly, Goodman was one of the first band leaders to lead an integrated band during the segregation era."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 1: "Flying Home", Benny Goodman, Charlie Christian, and Lionel Hampton

podcast.title: Progressive Stance on Integration
podcast.body: Goodman’s inclusion of black musicians, notably Teddy Wilson when Goodman was arguably the most popular musician in the USA, was a genuinely progressive statement for his time. Colonel Hampton later quoted Goodman as saying, "we need both the Black keys and the White keys to play music," an assertion made 80 years ago that predates similar well-meaning liberal comparisons. "So Goodman saying it 80 years ago, there's a genuinely progressive statement for the time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Rivalry with Chick Webb
podcast.body: Benny Goodman's band engaged in a notable rivalry with Chick Webb's band, culminating in a 1937 cutting contest at the Savoy Ballroom where Webb's band won. "Goodman's band was bigger, in every sense, but Webb's band was more popular with those who knew the real deal when they heard it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Small Group Head Arrangements
podcast.body: While Benny Goodman claimed responsibility for the head arrangements used by his small groups, many people believe that Charlie Christian was actually responsible for them. The sextet's music notably possessed a much more exhilarating feel compared to Goodman's earlier quartet or trio work. "While Goodman claimed responsibility for the head arrangements the small groups used, a lot of people think the Christian was responsible for these too, and certainly the sex-tats music has a much more exhilarating feel than the early quartet or trio work."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Support for Moondog's Lawsuit
podcast.body: Big band leader Benny Goodman assisted Moondog (Louis Hardin Jr.) in his lawsuit against disc jockey Allan Freed for the unauthorized use of the "Moon Dog" name. His support was instrumental in Moondog winning the case and securing damages and a promise from Freed to cease using the name. "so with the help of big band leader Benny Goodman, he sued Alan Fried, and he won six thousand dollars in damages."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Unison Riff Innovation on Flying Home
podcast.body: The main riff of "Flying Home" features a profound clarinet and an electric guitar playing the same riff in unison, a sound that had never been recorded before its 1939 release. This unusual combination created a unique harmonic tension from the outset. "This is a very profound, acclarenet, and an electric guitar, all playing the same riff in unison. That's a sound that had never been recorded before."

xref.title: Discovery by John Hammond
xref.body: John Hammond, a talent scout for Benny Goodman's Big Band Orchestra, convinced Benny Goodman to give Charlie Christian an audition, despite Goodman's initial skepticism about the electric guitar. Goodman was ultimately impressed by Christian's skill on the Gibson ES150. "John Hammond, a talent scout for Benny Goodman's Big Band Orchestra, armed twisted Benny into giving Charlie a shot. Goodman wasn't really into it because, well, who the hell wants to hear an electric guitar, he apparently said. But because Goodman trusted Hammond, he agreed to at least listen to Charlie. He was blown away by his abilities on this new instrument, which was a Gibson ES150 Spanish-style electric guitar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 1

xref.title: Early Electric Guitar Soloing
xref.body: Charlie Christian was an excellent guitarist who saw the potential for the electric guitar beyond chords and rhythm. He started improvising solos in jam sessions as early as 1931 and, after joining Benny Goodman's big band in 1939, was given the freedom to solo extensively, transforming the amplified guitar's role. "In 1931, he started soloing during jam sessions with fellow musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

xref.title: First Guitar Hero
xref.body: Charlie Christian, a Black man from Oklahoma, is recognized as the world's first guitar hero for his pioneering use of the electric guitar. He began soloing during jam sessions in 1931, acquired an electric guitar in 1936, and by 1939 with Benny Goodman's big band, was allowed to improvise and solo during performances, laying the foundations for the lead guitarist role. "So by every measure you want to use, Charlie Christian was the world's first guitar hero."

xref.title: Jazz Standards Repertoire
xref.body: As Jimmy Chamberlin's main gig from the age of 15, JP and the Cats played a repertoire rich in jazz standards. Their performances included works by renowned artists such as Benny Goodman, Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, and Gene Krupa, connecting the group to the big band era of the 1930s and 1940s. "His main gig was with a group called JP and the Cats, lots of standards by Benny Goodman and Count Basie and Tommy Dorsey, Jean Crouppa, and many other legends of the 30s and 40s."

xref.title: Lawsuit Against Allan Freed
xref.body: Moondog, incensed by disc jockey Allan Freed's unauthorized use of his "Moon Dog" moniker and "Moon Dog Symphony" as a radio show theme, sued Freed with the help of big band leader Benny Goodman. Moondog won the lawsuit, securing $6,000 in damages and a promise that Freed would never use the name "Moon Dog" again, directly influencing Freed's adoption of "rock and roll" as a descriptive term for the new music. "The actual Moon Dog was, as you might guess, incensed, so with the help of big band leader Benny Goodman, he sued Alan Fried, and he won six thousand dollars in damages."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Teenage Big Band Performer
xref.body: Jimmy Chamberlin demonstrated exceptional talent from a young age, starting to work in touring big bands when he was just 15. His primary engagement was with a group called JP and the Cats, where he performed numerous standards by legends such as Benny Goodman, Count Basie, Tommy Dorsey, and Gene Krupa, connecting him directly to the music of the 1930s and 1940s. "His main gig was with a group called JP and the Cats, lots of standards by Benny Goodman and Count Basie and Tommy Dorsey, Jean Crouppa, and many other legends of the 30s and 40s."
